nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Hardhead catfish
Scientific Name: Arius felis

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthys
	Order:  Cypriniformes
	Family:  Ariidae

Other Common Names:  silver catfish (834 957); large mouthed cat (834); gaff-topsail cat (791 834); sea catfish (70 116 255 327 581 789); tourist trout (327); smallmouth catfish (857); gafftop (664).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Not sought commercially, becomes entangled in nets and pump hoses.  Not reported separately in Florida landings data, but lumped with other catfish species (902).  Contributes small portion (2 - 3%) to the industrial bottom fish fishery of Louisiana and Mississippi which uses trash fish to produce pet food, fish meal, oil, and protein supplements for animal feeds, but is frequently discarded due to animals ingesting spines (47 193 285 605 695).  Catch statistics are probably underestimated because a large portion of the catch is discarded (193 605 857 908 1042).  Used briefly as a food fish during World War I and in 1943 (255), and where currently sold, it is usually marketed fresh (791).  Hardhead catfish made up between 1% and 3% of the industrial bottom fish catch in the north central Gulf of Mexico from 1959 to 1972 (193 605).  Nutritive value compares favorably with croaker, spot, and spotted sea trout, but attempts to market it as human food have failed because meat is dark and often has an offensive odor (47).

Recreational:  Not fished for by sportsmen, but frequently caught and then discarded by fishermen who detest it due to its venomous spines, undesirable flesh, and the difficulty in removing it from their line (19 255 282 327 695).  Angler surveys probably underestimate abundance, catch rates, and harvest for the species (857). Fishery information for the Gulf of Mexico showed a combined recreational catch of 18,474,000 saltwater catfishes in 1988 (513).  Muncy and Wingo (857) provided a review of catch rates in the northern Gulf of Mexico.  Although edible, this fish is generally not consumed (788), partly due to its reputation of feeding on any organic matter available (226).  Live catfish are used as bait for cobia at offshore oil rigs (857).

Ecological Role:  Opportunistic feeder with a capacity to utilize several different food sources (908).  This ability probably accounts for the successful adaptation of the sea catfish to different habitats (47 163 179 190 294 304 327).  Not an important forage organism, and competes with sport fishes for space and food (857).  Important in estuarine ecosystems as a scavenger (751).

Indicator:  Feeding behavior was not altered by exposure to fuel oil concentrations of 0.02 ml/l, but at 0.08 ml/l caused regurgitation of food and the loss of mucus layers in the stomach (1060).  Fuel oil concentrations of 0.01 ml/l caused slowed heart rates, and LD 50 at 96 hours has been reported as 0.14 ml fuel/l water (1060).  Used in research funded by the National Science Foundation to study the effects of sub-lethal copper exposure on marine fish (626).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Atlantic coastal waters from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to Yucatan, Mexico (366 381 788 791 851), but rare north of North Carolina (381).  Also in the northern Gulf of Mexico from south Florida to Yucatan (791 857).  Most abundant in brackish and marine waters, but also enters freshwater (264 265 515 790 791).  Widespread throughout range.

Within Study Area:  One of the most ubiquitous fishes present in the brackish and salt waters of the bays and shallow waters of the northern Gulf of Mexico (140 255 282).  Common in all coastal and estuarine waters of Florida.  Reported as common in most types of habitats in the Indian River Lagoon (848 887), abundant in the freshwater areas of North River in the Everglades (515), very common in the Charlotte Harbor area (789), commonly caught in the Tampa Bay area (664), and abundant (more abundant than B. marinus) at Cedar Key (581).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
One of the most abundant, shallow water species along the southeastern United States.  Eggs and yolksac larvae carried in mouth of male (857 908); demersal when dropped by parent (256).  Juveniles and adults demersal showing predominately nocturnal activity (163 179 190 282 328 674 675 786) with some diurnal activity, possibly attributed to differences in life cycle stages or seasonal variation (328 485).  Often found in schools (47 252 366) which may be formed and maintained by specific vocalizations (714).

Movements/Migrations:  Generally decrease in abundance in bays and estuaries along the northern Gulf of Mexico and Texas coast during fall and winter moving to deeper waters of the Gulf or sometimes within the estuary system to overwinter and then returning during spring and summer (223 255 399 325 372 550 675 694).  Older age class fish are reported to migrate while many of the younger ones remain in the bays (694).  Migration to Gulf can begin as early as September with lowest numbers in bay systems occurring from November to February (694 751).  Abundance increases with temperature (751 709) with returns to the bays and estuaries beginning from March to April and peak abundance being observed from April and May to as late as October along with a high influx of class 0 fish (19 104 115 116 140 294 328 372 373 548 550 646 751 786).  Migration is thought to be due to an endogenous mechanism entrained by photoperiod (674 675), but temperature also plays a role in controlling seasonal migration (372 550 694).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Egg/larvae: Eggs and yolk-sack larvae are carried in the mouth by adult males usually in shallow oligohaline to mesohaline waters of bays, lagoons, or Gulf inlets (39 80 256 407 756 786 857 908).

Juveniles: Taken from fresh to euhaline salinities in waters 0.6 to 3.0 m in depth (193 325 694).  Apparently more numerous than adults in waters of low salinity (256).

Adults: Taken from fresh to hypersaline waters.  Specimens taken at depths from 0.6 to 91.4 m but principally at 4 to 7 m (47 140 193 223 256 303 651 321 325 407 470 550 553 694).  Prefer warm waters in shallow grassy areas of bays and Gulf (47 140 115 223 294 325 327 407 467 786).

Substrate: Juveniles and adults have mostly been found over bottoms of mud, oyster beds, sand, shell, sandy mud, silt, and sand with shell (265 407 325 581 582 791 694).  Juveniles have been reported not to use grass beds (786) although adult have been found in areas with seagrass and detritus substrates.  Reported to be more abundant in areas with high organic substrates (1061 583).  Known to feed over mud bottoms and submerged sand flats (908).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae:  Eggs observed in both lab and field at a range of 28.0 to 34.0 C (116 255 550 756). Larvae have been taken in the field at 15.0 to 34.9 C (116 255 709).

Juveniles/Adult:  Both stages have been collected at temperatures ranging from 5.0 to 39.0 C (31 47 116 193 223 226 294 325 372 548 550 664 694 709 789).  Maximum acceptable temperature probably 37.0 C with 39.0 C being close to the upper lethal limit for this species (226).  Preference reported to be to be between 19.0 and 25.0 C (47), but adults also reported to prefer temperatures above 25.0 C (407).  Adults are said to leave shallow inshore waters for deeper channels or offshore areas when temperatures fall to 5.0 or 6.0 C (372 550 694).  Springer and Woodburn (664) found individuals in Tampa Bay that were swimming sluggishly and were easily captured by hand after the passage of a cold wave in December, 1957.  High mortality due to freezes has been reported at Sanibel Island, Florida (836).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae:  Collected in field over salinities ranging of 1.8 to 36.4 ppt (116 255). Collected from brooding males in salinities ranging from 2.0 to 36.0 ppt (80 116 140 550).

Juveniles/adults:  Free swimming juveniles collected from 0.05 to 56 ppt salinity, but reported to prefer <10.0 ppt (116 140 550).  Smaller individuals generally collected in least saline waters of Tampa Bay (664); few specimens have been collected in waters of less than 5.0 ppt (255).  Adults euryhaline, common from 0.0 to 45 ppt (31 80 116 140 193 223 255 256 261 294 321 372 325 546 548 651 664 694 696 709), but occur in salinities as high as 60 ppt (651).  Reported to show some preference for 15.0 to 30.0 ppt salinities and for numbers to decrease rapidly below 15 ppt (116 223 255 550 694 696).  Commonly occur in freshwater portions of coastal rivers in south Florida (790), at salinities ranging from 0.15 to 0.23 ppt in the St. Lucie River (264), in freshwaters of the Caloosahatchee River (265), and throughout the North River in south Florida during all seasons (515).

Dissolved Oxygen: Collected from waters with a D.O. range of 2.7 to 11.1 ppm (31 80).  Sometimes collected in habitats characterized by low D.O. (47).  Total oxygen depletion following the passage of a hurricane was reportedly the cause of catfish mortality in two south Florida bays (702)

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode:  Oviparous, gonochoristic, iteroparus, adults sexually dimorphic during and around breeding, fertilization is probably external; males mouth brood eggs and yolk-sac larvae.

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Adults reach sexual maturity before 2 years of age (47).  Size at first sexual maturity has been reported as ranging from 120 to 200 mm SL with most maturing at larger sizes; one gravid female measured 126mm SL and males probably mature at sizes around 250 mm SL (381 407).  Spawning apparently occurs from May to August or September in most of the northern Gulf of Mexico in waters 0.6 to 1.2 m deep (255 256 381 407 756 857).  Spawning occurs in shallow waters of secondary and primary bays, and Gulf inlets (38 80 255 256 374 407 582 751 756).  Although no spawning has been observed in the Gulf of Mexico, ripe females with large ovarian eggs were taken there in 21.9 to 27.4 m during July (303) and the absence of adults has been noted in some inshore areas during the spawning season (188 664).  Spawning females have hemorrhagic genital openings with the orifice slightly everted (256), and  enlarged pelvic fins which may serve to enhance fertilization (407).  The smallest size at which pelvic fin differences between males and females can be observed has been reported as 105mm SL (407).  Females with enlarging pelvic fins are seen as early as March and through July and do not totally disappear until after October (255).  Motile sperm in males has been noted from early March until the middle of July (756).  It has been suggested that eggs are initially deposited in sandy depressions and fertilized by the males that then pick them up into their mouths (256 366).  Brooding males have enlarged branchial and buccal cavities to accommodate eggs or larvae and their mouths are hemorrhagic in appearance (407 582 786).  Brooding males are observed from May to July (70 80 116 188 255 256 407 582 786).  Reports on the numbers of eggs or larvae found in brood males range from 1 to 48 with the length of the male appearing to have no connection with the number of eggs or larvae brooded (255 256 407 582 583).  Males fast during brooding period which lasts about 60 days (256 366 407).

Fecundity: Produces 14 to 64 mature ova each season along with numerous small, nonfunctional eggs (381 756); left ovary slightly larger and typically with 3 - 6 more eggs than right (255 256 366 407 582 756).  May spawn more than once a season (255).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Demersal; held in adult male's mouth.  Ripe ovarian eggs are greenish, slightly oval or elliptical, and measure 12 - 19 mm in diameter (256 366 407 582 756 857).  Many small nonfunctional eggs attached to ripe eggs and to each other by a thin colorless adhesive film that is lost as development proceeds.  Nonfunctional eggs may serve as food for males that fast while brooding (256 756).  After fertilization, at 29.5 to 30.5 C, eggs reach 2-cell stage at 4 hrs, 4-cell stage at 7 hrs, 8-cell stage at 9 hrs, and 16-cell stage at 11 hrs (756).  Fertilized eggs become blastulas at 20 hrs and gastrulas at 29 hrs (756). Hatching probably occurs in about 30 days (381).

Yolksac larvae:  Hatching size ranges from 29 - 45 mm TL and occurs primarily in June (80 140 226).  Duration of stage ranges from ca. 2 to 4 weeks in the wild and up to 55 days under laboratory conditions (366).  Fin ray complement complete before yolk absorption, therefore it is considered that no larval stage exists (366).  Yolk used up by 50 mm TL (255).

Juveniles:  Released by male parent from June to August (116 226 255 694).  Release size ranges from 33 to 58 mm SL (226) and 41 to 62 mm TL (116 255 694).  Reported growth in Galveston Bay ranged from 40 - 44 mm SL in July to 93 mm in October (226).  Juveniles in wild observed to grow 10 mm/mo from July to October, however, cooler water temperatures drastically reduced growth rate in winter (116).

Adults:  Maximum reported sizes are 635 mm TL and 330 mm SL (31 582) with average sizes of 100 to 160 mm FL (115 550).  Maximum weight reported as 5500 gm (12 lbs) (788), but rarely exceeds 1154 gm in weight (226).  Average life span 2 to 3 years (115 694), but a maximum life span of 5 years has also been reported (47).  Age determinations from pectoral spines of 177 individuals collected in Mississippi indicated that fish live from 3 to 8 growing seasons (1063).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Both juveniles and adults are opportunistic, nocturnal bottom feeders utilizing a wide range of feeding modes such as scavenging, carnivory, and ectoparasitism (47 163 179 190 282 294 304 323 467 515).  This species may pass through three feeding stages in its development: zooplankton, especially copepods, are most important for individuals <100 mm TL; micro-bottom invertebrates are most important for individuals between 100_200 mm TL; crabs and fishes gradually assume importance in fish >200 mm TL (163).  Specific diet items reported include: bottom debris and detritus; mysids, insects, arachnids, plant tissue, algae, polychaetes, ostracods, isopods, copepods, cirripedia, amphipods, Penaeus sp., Penaeus aztecus, Penaeus duorarum, Palaemonetes sp., Callinectes sapidus, xanthid crabs, gastropods, Brevoortia sp., Anchoa sp., Menidia sp., Mugil sp., Panopeus sp., juvenile Arius felis, eggs and cysts, hermit crabs, bivalves, nudibranchs, fish bones, and scales actively taken from living fish (163 179 255 282 294 303 323 327 467 582 584 664).  No live fish are apparently ingested (664), but females have been known to occasionally feed on their own eggs (407).  Evidence of lepidophogy, or scale feeding, primarily by juvenile catfish, has been presented by Hoese (323) and Springer and Woodburn (664).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Opportunistic feeder with a capacity to utilize several different food sources (908).  This ability probably accounts for the successful adaptation of the sea catfish to different habitats (47 163 179 190 294 304 327).  Important in estuarine ecosystems as a scavenger (751).  Sea catfish have been reported as prey for Lepisosteus osseus, Rachycentron canadum, Carcharhinus leucas, Epinephelus itajara, Elops saurus, Cynoscion nebulosus, and Sciaenops ocellatus (62 165 255 467).  Nematodes have been observed to parasitize sea catfish in blister like swellings under the skin of the caudal region (255).  Studies have demonstrated that sounds emitted by the sea catfish could enable them to avoid obstructions, and probably predators, at close range.  Sounds may also be used to communicate during breeding and nocturnal schooling (67 714 715 716).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title:  Hardhead Catfish (Arius felis)

FLELMR CODE:  1301

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
1993 Jan 19. REB; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
3/1/94.  REB; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Hardhead catfish
Scientific Name: Arius felis

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthys
	Order:  Cypriniformes
	Family:  Ariidae

Other Common Names:  silver catfish (834 957); large mouthed cat (834); gaff-topsail cat (791 834); sea catfish (70 116 255 327 581 789); tourist trout (327); smallmouth catfish (857); gafftop (664).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Not sought commercially, becomes entangled in nets and pump hoses.  Not reported separately in Florida landings data, but lumped with other catfish species (902).  Contributes small portion (2 - 3%) to the industrial bottom fish fishery of Louisiana and Mississippi which uses trash fish to produce pet food, fish meal, oil, and protein supplements for animal feeds, but is frequently discarded due to animals ingesting spines (47 193 285 605 695).  Catch statistics are probably underestimated because a large portion of the catch is discarded (193 605 857 908 1042).  Used briefly as a food fish during World War I and in 1943 (255), and where currently sold, it is usually marketed fresh (791).  Hardhead catfish made up between 1% and 3% of the industrial bottom fish catch in the north central Gulf of Mexico from 1959 to 1972 (193 605).  Nutritive value compares favorably with croaker, spot, and spotted sea trout, but attempts to market it as human food have failed because meat is dark and often has an offensive odor (47).

Recreational:  Not fished for by sportsmen, but frequently caught and then discarded by fishermen who detest it due to its venomous spines, undesirable flesh, and the difficulty in removing it from their line (19 255 282 327 695).  Angler surveys probably underestimate abundance, catch rates, and harvest for the species (857). Fishery information for the Gulf of Mexico showed a combined recreational catch of 18,474,000 saltwater catfishes in 1988 (513).  Muncy and Wingo (857) provided a review of catch rates in the northern Gulf of Mexico.  Although edible, this fish is generally not consumed (788), partly due to its reputation of feeding on any organic matter available (226).  Live catfish are used as bait for cobia at offshore oil rigs (857).

Ecological Role:  Opportunistic feeder with a capacity to utilize several different food sources (908).  This ability probably accounts for the successful adaptation of the sea catfish to different habitats (47 163 179 190 294 304 327).  Not an important forage organism, and competes with sport fishes for space and food (857).  Important in estuarine ecosystems as a scavenger (751).

Indicator:  Feeding behavior was not altered by exposure to fuel oil concentrations of 0.02 ml/l, but at 0.08 ml/l caused regurgitation of food and the loss of mucus layers in the stomach (1060).  Fuel oil concentrations of 0.01 ml/l caused slowed heart rates, and LD 50 at 96 hours has been reported as 0.14 ml fuel/l water (1060).  Used in research funded by the National Science Foundation to study the effects of sub-lethal copper exposure on marine fish (626).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Atlantic coastal waters from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to Yucatan, Mexico (366 381 788 791 851), but rare north of North Carolina (381).  Also in the northern Gulf of Mexico from south Florida to Yucatan (791 857).  Most abundant in brackish and marine waters, but also enters freshwater (264 265 515 790 791).  Widespread throughout range.

Within Study Area:  One of the most ubiquitous fishes present in the brackish and salt waters of the bays and shallow waters of the northern Gulf of Mexico (140 255 282).  Common in all coastal and estuarine waters of Florida.  Reported as common in most types of habitats in the Indian River Lagoon (848 887), abundant in the freshwater areas of North River in the Everglades (515), very common in the Charlotte Harbor area (789), commonly caught in the Tampa Bay area (664), and abundant (more abundant than B. marinus) at Cedar Key (581).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
One of the most abundant, shallow water species along the southeastern United States.  Eggs and yolksac larvae carried in mouth of male (857 908); demersal when dropped by parent (256).  Juveniles and adults demersal showing predominately nocturnal activity (163 179 190 282 328 674 675 786) with some diurnal activity, possibly attributed to differences in life cycle stages or seasonal variation (328 485).  Often found in schools (47 252 366) which may be formed and maintained by specific vocalizations (714).

Movements/Migrations:  Generally decrease in abundance in bays and estuaries along the northern Gulf of Mexico and Texas coast during fall and winter moving to deeper waters of the Gulf or sometimes within the estuary system to overwinter and then returning during spring and summer (223 255 399 325 372 550 675 694).  Older age class fish are reported to migrate while many of the younger ones remain in the bays (694).  Migration to Gulf can begin as early as September with lowest numbers in bay systems occurring from November to February (694 751).  Abundance increases with temperature (751 709) with returns to the bays and estuaries beginning from March to April and peak abundance being observed from April and May to as late as October along with a high influx of class 0 fish (19 104 115 116 140 294 328 372 373 548 550 646 751 786).  Migration is thought to be due to an endogenous mechanism entrained by photoperiod (674 675), but temperature also plays a role in controlling seasonal migration (372 550 694).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Egg/larvae: Eggs and yolk-sack larvae are carried in the mouth by adult males usually in shallow oligohaline to mesohaline waters of bays, lagoons, or Gulf inlets (39 80 256 407 756 786 857 908).

Juveniles: Taken from fresh to euhaline salinities in waters 0.6 to 3.0 m in depth (193 325 694).  Apparently more numerous than adults in waters of low salinity (256).

Adults: Taken from fresh to hypersaline waters.  Specimens taken at depths from 0.6 to 91.4 m but principally at 4 to 7 m (47 140 193 223 256 303 651 321 325 407 470 550 553 694).  Prefer warm waters in shallow grassy areas of bays and Gulf (47 140 115 223 294 325 327 407 467 786).

Substrate: Juveniles and adults have mostly been found over bottoms of mud, oyster beds, sand, shell, sandy mud, silt, and sand with shell (265 407 325 581 582 791 694).  Juveniles have been reported not to use grass beds (786) although adult have been found in areas with seagrass and detritus substrates.  Reported to be more abundant in areas with high organic substrates (1061 583).  Known to feed over mud bottoms and submerged sand flats (908).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs/larvae:  Eggs observed in both lab and field at a range of 28.0 to 34.0 C (116 255 550 756). Larvae have been taken in the field at 15.0 to 34.9 C (116 255 709).

Juveniles/Adult:  Both stages have been collected at temperatures ranging from 5.0 to 39.0 C (31 47 116 193 223 226 294 325 372 548 550 664 694 709 789).  Maximum acceptable temperature probably 37.0 C with 39.0 C being close to the upper lethal limit for this species (226).  Preference reported to be to be between 19.0 and 25.0 C (47), but adults also reported to prefer temperatures above 25.0 C (407).  Adults are said to leave shallow inshore waters for deeper channels or offshore areas when temperatures fall to 5.0 or 6.0 C (372 550 694).  Springer and Woodburn (664) found individuals in Tampa Bay that were swimming sluggishly and were easily captured by hand after the passage of a cold wave in December, 1957.  High mortality due to freezes has been reported at Sanibel Island, Florida (836).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Eggs/larvae:  Collected in field over salinities ranging of 1.8 to 36.4 ppt (116 255). Collected from brooding males in salinities ranging from 2.0 to 36.0 ppt (80 116 140 550).

Juveniles/adults:  Free swimming juveniles collected from 0.05 to 56 ppt salinity, but reported to prefer <10.0 ppt (116 140 550).  Smaller individuals generally collected in least saline waters of Tampa Bay (664); few specimens have been collected in waters of less than 5.0 ppt (255).  Adults euryhaline, common from 0.0 to 45 ppt (31 80 116 140 193 223 255 256 261 294 321 372 325 546 548 651 664 694 696 709), but occur in salinities as high as 60 ppt (651).  Reported to show some preference for 15.0 to 30.0 ppt salinities and for numbers to decrease rapidly below 15 ppt (116 223 255 550 694 696).  Commonly occur in freshwater portions of coastal rivers in south Florida (790), at salinities ranging from 0.15 to 0.23 ppt in the St. Lucie River (264), in freshwaters of the Caloosahatchee River (265), and throughout the North River in south Florida during all seasons (515).

Dissolved Oxygen: Collected from waters with a D.O. range of 2.7 to 11.1 ppm (31 80).  Sometimes collected in habitats characterized by low D.O. (47).  Total oxygen depletion following the passage of a hurricane was reportedly the cause of catfish mortality in two south Florida bays (702)

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content: Reproductive Mode:  Oviparous, gonochoristic, iteroparus, adults sexually dimorphic during and around breeding, fertilization is probably external; males mouth brood eggs and yolk-sac larvae.

sections.heading: Mating/Spawning
sections.content:
Adults reach sexual maturity before 2 years of age (47).  Size at first sexual maturity has been reported as ranging from 120 to 200 mm SL with most maturing at larger sizes; one gravid female measured 126mm SL and males probably mature at sizes around 250 mm SL (381 407).  Spawning apparently occurs from May to August or September in most of the northern Gulf of Mexico in waters 0.6 to 1.2 m deep (255 256 381 407 756 857).  Spawning occurs in shallow waters of secondary and primary bays, and Gulf inlets (38 80 255 256 374 407 582 751 756).  Although no spawning has been observed in the Gulf of Mexico, ripe females with large ovarian eggs were taken there in 21.9 to 27.4 m during July (303) and the absence of adults has been noted in some inshore areas during the spawning season (188 664).  Spawning females have hemorrhagic genital openings with the orifice slightly everted (256), and  enlarged pelvic fins which may serve to enhance fertilization (407).  The smallest size at which pelvic fin differences between males and females can be observed has been reported as 105mm SL (407).  Females with enlarging pelvic fins are seen as early as March and through July and do not totally disappear until after October (255).  Motile sperm in males has been noted from early March until the middle of July (756).  It has been suggested that eggs are initially deposited in sandy depressions and fertilized by the males that then pick them up into their mouths (256 366).  Brooding males have enlarged branchial and buccal cavities to accommodate eggs or larvae and their mouths are hemorrhagic in appearance (407 582 786).  Brooding males are observed from May to July (70 80 116 188 255 256 407 582 786).  Reports on the numbers of eggs or larvae found in brood males range from 1 to 48 with the length of the male appearing to have no connection with the number of eggs or larvae brooded (255 256 407 582 583).  Males fast during brooding period which lasts about 60 days (256 366 407).

Fecundity: Produces 14 to 64 mature ova each season along with numerous small, nonfunctional eggs (381 756); left ovary slightly larger and typically with 3 - 6 more eggs than right (255 256 366 407 582 756).  May spawn more than once a season (255).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Demersal; held in adult male's mouth.  Ripe ovarian eggs are greenish, slightly oval or elliptical, and measure 12 - 19 mm in diameter (256 366 407 582 756 857).  Many small nonfunctional eggs attached to ripe eggs and to each other by a thin colorless adhesive film that is lost as development proceeds.  Nonfunctional eggs may serve as food for males that fast while brooding (256 756).  After fertilization, at 29.5 to 30.5 C, eggs reach 2-cell stage at 4 hrs, 4-cell stage at 7 hrs, 8-cell stage at 9 hrs, and 16-cell stage at 11 hrs (756).  Fertilized eggs become blastulas at 20 hrs and gastrulas at 29 hrs (756). Hatching probably occurs in about 30 days (381).

Yolksac larvae:  Hatching size ranges from 29 - 45 mm TL and occurs primarily in June (80 140 226).  Duration of stage ranges from ca. 2 to 4 weeks in the wild and up to 55 days under laboratory conditions (366).  Fin ray complement complete before yolk absorption, therefore it is considered that no larval stage exists (366).  Yolk used up by 50 mm TL (255).

Juveniles:  Released by male parent from June to August (116 226 255 694).  Release size ranges from 33 to 58 mm SL (226) and 41 to 62 mm TL (116 255 694).  Reported growth in Galveston Bay ranged from 40 - 44 mm SL in July to 93 mm in October (226).  Juveniles in wild observed to grow 10 mm/mo from July to October, however, cooler water temperatures drastically reduced growth rate in winter (116).

Adults:  Maximum reported sizes are 635 mm TL and 330 mm SL (31 582) with average sizes of 100 to 160 mm FL (115 550).  Maximum weight reported as 5500 gm (12 lbs) (788), but rarely exceeds 1154 gm in weight (226).  Average life span 2 to 3 years (115 694), but a maximum life span of 5 years has also been reported (47).  Age determinations from pectoral spines of 177 individuals collected in Mississippi indicated that fish live from 3 to 8 growing seasons (1063).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Both juveniles and adults are opportunistic, nocturnal bottom feeders utilizing a wide range of feeding modes such as scavenging, carnivory, and ectoparasitism (47 163 179 190 282 294 304 323 467 515).  This species may pass through three feeding stages in its development: zooplankton, especially copepods, are most important for individuals <100 mm TL; micro-bottom invertebrates are most important for individuals between 100_200 mm TL; crabs and fishes gradually assume importance in fish >200 mm TL (163).  Specific diet items reported include: bottom debris and detritus; mysids, insects, arachnids, plant tissue, algae, polychaetes, ostracods, isopods, copepods, cirripedia, amphipods, Penaeus sp., Penaeus aztecus, Penaeus duorarum, Palaemonetes sp., Callinectes sapidus, xanthid crabs, gastropods, Brevoortia sp., Anchoa sp., Menidia sp., Mugil sp., Panopeus sp., juvenile Arius felis, eggs and cysts, hermit crabs, bivalves, nudibranchs, fish bones, and scales actively taken from living fish (163 179 255 282 294 303 323 327 467 582 584 664).  No live fish are apparently ingested (664), but females have been known to occasionally feed on their own eggs (407).  Evidence of lepidophogy, or scale feeding, primarily by juvenile catfish, has been presented by Hoese (323) and Springer and Woodburn (664).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Opportunistic feeder with a capacity to utilize several different food sources (908).  This ability probably accounts for the successful adaptation of the sea catfish to different habitats (47 163 179 190 294 304 327).  Important in estuarine ecosystems as a scavenger (751).  Sea catfish have been reported as prey for Lepisosteus osseus, Rachycentron canadum, Carcharhinus leucas, Epinephelus itajara, Elops saurus, Cynoscion nebulosus, and Sciaenops ocellatus (62 165 255 467).  Nematodes have been observed to parasitize sea catfish in blister like swellings under the skin of the caudal region (255).  Studies have demonstrated that sounds emitted by the sea catfish could enable them to avoid obstructions, and probably predators, at close range.  Sounds may also be used to communicate during breeding and nocturnal schooling (67 714 715 716).
